analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 94 cosponsors but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax — the tax owed when someone dies leaving a very large fortune — along with the gift tax and the tax on transfers that skip a generation. Today only the largest estates owe any estate tax at all, so the bill's benefits would go almost entirely to the heirs of the wealthiest families, while the government would have to make up the lost revenue through other taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates would gain the most. The estate tax applies only after an estate exceeds a sizable exemption — millions of dollars per person — so the vast majority of families never pay it. Repeal would concentrate its savings among the few thousand largest estates each year, and because the gift tax would also be repealed, wealthy families could transfer fortunes during life completely tax-free. Wealth-management and estate-planning firms would lose a core line of business.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax regime by striking Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code.
The repeal applies to deaths, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers occurring after enactment, so large estates could pass to heirs free of federal estate tax.
Because the gift tax is repealed at the same time, the wealthiest families could give assets to children and grandchildren during their lifetimes without any federal transfer tax.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose a tax paid almost exclusively by multimillion-dollar estates. That revenue would have to be replaced by higher taxes on others, more federal borrowing, or cuts to government services — a cost spread across ordinary taxpayers. Without the estate tax, large fortunes could also pass untaxed from generation to generation, concentrating wealth further.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes eliminates a federal revenue stream drawn from the largest estates, which must be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or spending reductions.

The estate tax only applies to estates above a large exemption, so repeal delivers its savings to the heirs of the wealthiest families rather than to typical households, and repealing the gift tax alongside it allows unlimited lifetime tax-free transfers.

A good-faith supporter's cost to acknowledge: family farms and small businesses are the oft-cited reason for repeal, but because the tax already exempts the vast majority of estates, most farm and small-business families owe nothing and repeal spends most of its money on the very largest fortunes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit falls on a small group — heirs of the largest estates — while the cost is a permanent loss of federal revenue that everyone else must absorb. The estate tax already exempts nearly all family farms and small businesses through its exemption and special valuation rules, so the bill's central benefit goes to the very largest fortunes rather than to the family businesses most often cited in its favor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee in March 2007, the committee never considered it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act of 2007 on March 20, 2007.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
The bill attracted 94 cosponsors — 93 Republicans and 1 Democrat.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died at the end of the 110th Congress in January 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off that the bill died: the estate tax, which is owed only on very large estates, remained in place, preserving federal revenue and the only direct federal tax on inherited wealth. Wealthy families who hoped to pass estates tax-free did not get that change.

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

for.name: 93 of 94 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal, signaling majority-Republican House support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, keeping the bill from reaching the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the tax-writing committee, never acted on the bill during the 110th Congress.

against.name: House Democratic majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House calendar in the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled the chamber after the 2006 elections and did not advance the estate tax repeal.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Republican: of the bill's 94 cosponsors, 93 were Republicans and 1 was a Democrat, while the Democratic House majority never brought the bill up.

industries.industry: Heirs and estates of the wealthiest households
industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated the only federal tax on very large inherited fortunes, a burden borne by a small number of multimillion-dollar estates. The lost revenue would fall back on other taxpayers.
These firms sell complex planning to manage estate and gift tax exposure; full repeal would remove much of that business. Their loss would come alongside a tax cut for the very wealthy.
A major use of life insurance is providing cash to pay estate taxes; repeal of the estate tax would shrink that market. Ordinary policyholders would see no offsetting gain.
